staged_source_snapshot.description: Stage 01 reproduced against this checked-out vulnerable snapshot. The sample metadata labels vulnerable commit `da436e53d06318e92ba99e731f6772808dcc66c3`, but the source used for this trace is the staged workspace commit above; its `sam.c` and `hts.c` line locations match the saved ASan trace and the staged patch exactly.

bug_description.original: OSS-Fuzz issue 42479042 (htslib): Heap-buffer-overflow READ {*} found by fuzz target hts_open_fuzzer [asan]. https://issues.oss-fuzz.com/issues/42479042
bug_description.original_source: sample_info.json / sanitizer_trace.txt / default_crash_trace.txt / reproduction_report.json / patch.diff / staged vulnerable source
bug_description.normalized: The staged 165-byte witness is a malformed BAM file whose first alignment record materializes `block_len = 73`, `l_qname = 16`, `n_cigar = 2`, and `l_qseq = 10`. `bam_read1()` therefore computes `l_extranul = 0`, allocates `new_l_data = 41` bytes for the record payload, and `sam_realloc_bam_data()` rounds that request up to the 64-byte heap region reported by ASan. The first 16 payload bytes read into `b->data` are qname bytes `0xb0 * 16`, so `b->data[c->l_qname - 1]` is not `\0`, but the vulnerable code performs no post-read qname-termination check before later exposing `b->data` via `bam_get_qname(b)`. Because `l_extranul == 0`, the padding loop writes no NUL byte; the remaining 25 bytes of this logical record are also all non-zero. The same record's malformed CIGAR words are both `0xb0b0b0b0`, so `bam_cigar2rqlens()` derives `qlen = 370546198`, which disagrees with `l_qseq = 10`. That mismatch takes the logging path in `bam_read1()`, and `hts_log()` forwards `bam_get_qname(b)` to `vfprintf` as a `%s` argument. In the reproduced ASan run, no terminator was encountered before the end of the 64-byte allocation, so the formatting scan crossed into the right redzone and AddressSanitizer reported a heap-buffer-overflow read of size 65. The staged fixing patch adds an explicit `b->data[c->l_qname - 1] != '\0'` check and `fixup_missing_qname_nul(b)` repair immediately after the qname read, closing that missing post-read obligation.

source.description: First project parser/load step for the vulnerable BAM record. `bam_read1()` reads the first record header from the attacker-controlled stream and materializes the record-length and BAM core fields that drive the vulnerable path.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` is a 165-byte BAM file. Its first alignment record begins at file offset 15; the 4-byte record-length field there is `0x49` (`73`), and the following 32-byte BAM core header yields `l_qname = 16`, `n_cigar = 2`, and `l_qseq = 10` when parsed by this code.
source.note: Source. This block is the first project-code statement sequence that consumes the witness bytes into the BAM record state later used by the qname load, CIGAR sanity check, and log sink.

relation.description: Source identity relation for the vulnerability-relevant value.

sink.description: Closest project sink to the ASan crash. `vfprintf` consumes the `%s` argument supplied by `bam_read1()` and scans the unterminated `bam_get_qname(b)` pointer until it crosses the 64-byte heap allocation for `b->data`.
sink.note: ASan reports the read in `printf_common`, but the closest project-level sink is `hts_log()`'s call to `vfprintf(stderr, format, argptr);`.

root_cause.description: Root cause. After reading `c->l_qname` bytes of qname data into `b->data`, the vulnerable code never verifies that `b->data[c->l_qname - 1]` is `\0` before later exposing the buffer via `bam_get_qname(b)`.
root_cause.note: The staged patch inserts `if (b->data[c->l_qname - 1] != '\0') { if (fixup_missing_qname_nul(b) < 0) return -4; }` immediately after this line, which is exactly the missing post-read validation and repair.

tainted_value_origin.description: The first concrete vulnerability-relevant values are the parsed BAM core fields. `l_qname = 16` determines the qname read length and, because it is 4-byte aligned, makes `l_extranul` become zero. `n_cigar = 2` and `l_qseq = 10` later make the CIGAR/query-length sanity check reach the logging path.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: Static parsing of the staged witness yields `l_qname = 16`, `n_cigar = 2`, and `l_qseq = 10` from the first alignment record's 32-byte core header.

parser_admitted.description: Structural BAM-size checkpoint. For the staged first record, `((2 << 2) + 16 + 0 + ((10 + 1) >> 1) + 10) = 39`, which is `<= new_l_data = 41`, so the malformed record passes `bam_read1()`'s size checks and reaches the vulnerable qname-loading path.

fine_trace.note: Source. `bam_read1()` reads the first BAM alignment header from the attacker-controlled stream and materializes the values that drive the vulnerable path. Static parsing of the staged witness yields `block_len = 73`, `l_qname = 16`, `n_cigar = 2`, and `l_qseq = 10` for this first record.

Derives how many alignment-padding NUL bytes can follow the qname. Because the witness sets `l_qname = 16` and `16 % 4 == 0`, this computes `l_extranul = 0`, so the record has no padding byte that could incidentally terminate an unterminated qname.

fine_trace.var: block_len, new_l_data, c->n_cigar, c->l_qname, c->l_extranul, c->l_qseq
fine_trace.note: Computes the logical size of the record payload and checks that the parsed BAM lengths are self-consistent. With `block_len = 73` from step 1 and `l_extranul = 0` from step 2, `new_l_data = 41`; the structural guard also passes because the parsed components require 39 bytes, so the malformed record is accepted instead of rejected.

Allocates storage for the record payload and records the logical data length. `new_l_data` is 41, and `sam_realloc_bam_data()` rounds that request up with `kroundup32`, matching ASan's report that `b->data` points to a 64-byte heap region.

Root cause. This statement reads the qname bytes into the start of `b->data`. For the staged witness, those 16 qname bytes are all `0xb0`, so `b->data[15]` is not `\0`. The vulnerable code still performs no post-read termination check here, leaving `bam_get_qname(b)` unterminated from the moment these bytes are stored.

Completes the record payload after the qname. Because `l_extranul = 0`, the padding loop writes no NUL byte and `c->l_qname` stays 16; the subsequent read appends the remaining 25 attacker-controlled bytes of the record. In the staged witness those 25 bytes are also all non-zero, so the entire 41-byte logical record buffer contains no terminator.

Decodes the query length implied by the record's malformed CIGAR words. The staged record stores two CIGAR entries `0xb0b0b0b0`, so `bam_cigar2rqlens()` derives `qlen = 370546198`, far larger than the parsed `l_qseq = 10`.

The sanity-check predicate that gates the error log evaluates true for the witness: `c->l_qseq > 0` (`10 > 0`), the record is not flagged unmapped, and the derived `qlen` from step 7 does not equal `c->l_qseq`. This takes execution into the logging branch that formats the qname as a C string.

fine_trace.code:
hts_log_error("CIGAR and query sequence lengths differ for %s",
        bam_get_qname(b));
fine_trace.note: Hands the qname to the logger as a `%s` argument. `bam_get_qname(b)` is the macro `(char *)(b)->data`, so this passes the start of the unterminated record buffer from steps 5-6 directly to the formatting code with C-string semantics.

ASan sink. `vfprintf` processes the `%s` argument from step 9 and keeps scanning the `bam_get_qname(b)` pointer for a terminating NUL. In the reproduced run, the scan traversed the entire 64-byte heap allocation for `b->data` without finding one and then read the 65th byte in the right redzone, producing the reported heap-buffer-overflow `READ of size 65`.

evidence_limitations: The staged artifacts let Stage 02 prove that the 41-byte logical BAM record payload contains no `\0` terminator. They do not preserve the allocator-rounding slack bytes between `b->l_data == 41` and ASan's 64-byte allocation; the saved ASan `READ of size 65` is the runtime evidence that `vfprintf` still found no terminator before the redzone.

allocation_context.note: The crashing string pointer lives in `b->data`, which is allocated by `realloc_bam_data(b, new_l_data)` at this call site. ASan reports the resulting heap object as a 64-byte region.

cross_validation.patch_resolves_note: The staged patch is source-grounded to this bug: it adds `fixup_missing_qname_nul()` and inserts `if (b->data[c->l_qname - 1] != '\0') { ... }` immediately after the qname read at `sam.c:578`, exactly where the vulnerable trace leaves `bam_get_qname(b)` unterminated. Stage 01 did not execute a fixed build for this sample, so `patch_resolves` remains false even though the patch matches the traced root cause.

poc.trigger: Stage 01's saved vulnerable run executed `PYTHONPATH=gt_generation python3 -m gt_toolkit arvo-workspace --result-dir /mnt/datastore/gt_generation/gt_results/arvo_42479042 run --version vulnerable --expect crash` and reproduced `AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 65` with stack `hts_log -> bam_read1 -> sam_read1 -> view_sam`, matching OSS-Fuzz issue 42479042.

format.name: Malformed BAM file read through hts_open_fuzzer
format.contract: The verified trigger is the exact 165-byte witness stored in `poc` (SHA-256 `3124af41a9c56fd99aa4beb5e8e47346e855d36abc0f0d43a0190c6d5ea94f28`). It begins with BAM magic and no reference sequences, and its first alignment record at file offset 15 has `block_len = 73`, `l_qname = 16`, `n_cigar = 2`, `l_qseq = 10`, qname bytes `0xb0 * 16`, and remaining record bytes `b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 f0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0 b0`, so the 41-byte logical record payload contains no `\0`. The two CIGAR words are both `0xb0b0b0b0`, yielding `qlen = 370546198`, which forces `bam_read1()` to execute `hts_log_error(..., bam_get_qname(b))`. Stage 01 only proves this exact blob; this contract does not generalize to nearby BAM headers, qname lengths, or alternate CIGAR values.
